title: How Would You Light a Fire on Titan?
description:
What Would Happen If You Landed on Titan? (Seas of Liquid Gas) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T3cBBss1F60

How would you light a fire on Saturn's largest moon, Titan? Titan has lakes of liquid hydrocarbon fuel and methane in its sky, yet almost no oxygen. Its atmosphere is about 95% nitrogen and 5% methane, compared with roughly 21% oxygen in Earth's air. If you struck a match or fired a rocket thruster in Titan's atmosphere, the fuel around you would not catch fire — to make a flame on Titan, you would have to carry a tank of oxygen on your back and spray it out into the methane sky.

Sources: NASA Science, Titan Facts — atmosphere composition (~95% nitrogen, ~5% methane) and liquid methane and ethane lakes (https://science.nasa.gov/saturn/moons/titan/facts/); NASA Science, Dragonfly Science — Titan's notable lack of oxygen (https://science.nasa.gov/mission/dragonfly/science/); ESA Cassini-Huygens — surface liquid hydrocarbons and lakes on Titan (https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Cassini-Huygens/Titan_s_surface_organics_surpass_oil_reserves_on_Earth); NASA NSSDCA, Earth Fact Sheet — Earth atmosphere composition (78.08% nitrogen, 20.95% oxygen) (https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html).

Image credits: NASA/Johns Hopkins APL/Goddard Space Flight Center/Steve Gribben (Dragonfly SVS 20311 animations and surface stills); NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASI/Cornell (Cassini Radar: PIA20021); NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/University of Idaho/DLR (Cassini VIMS: PIA21434); NASA/JPL-Caltech/Space Science Institute (Cassini ISS: PIA14922, PIA17177, PIA20016); NASA Johnson Space Center (Apollo 17 AS17-148-22727).

Pictures: Original animated explainers alongside NASA/ASI/APL imagery, with AI-assisted voice and editing. Facts: every number is checked against the sources listed above.
